name: Organic Chemistry
tagline: Synthetic routes, green chemistry, retrosynthesis, and molecular modeling.
seo_title: Organic Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Organic Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: daily paper summaries, field news and innovations in synthesis, catalysis, stereochemistry and retrosynthesis.

definition.lead: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds: how they are built, how they react, and how chemists make new ones.
definition.body: Carbon forms four strong bonds and bonds strongly to itself, so it can grow into chains, rings and 3D frameworks of almost any shape. That one property is why the same field covers fuels, plastics, dyes, DNA and nearly every medicine on a pharmacy shelf. The name is a fossil: it once meant 'compounds only living things can make', until chemists proved otherwise in 1828.

branches.name: Total synthesis
branches.summary: Building complex natural molecules from simple starting materials, step by step.
branches.example: Taxol, the anticancer drug from yew bark, has been synthesized by several groups.

branches.name: Retrosynthesis
branches.summary: Planning a synthesis backwards: cutting the target into simpler pieces until you reach things you can buy.
branches.example: AI tools now propose retrosynthetic routes in seconds.

branches.name: Reaction mechanisms
branches.summary: Following every electron movement to explain why a reaction happens and what it gives.
branches.example: Why SN2 inverts a stereocenter while SN1 scrambles it.

branches.name: Stereochemistry
branches.summary: The 3D arrangement of atoms, and making one mirror-image form selectively.
branches.example: One enantiomer of a drug can heal while the other does nothing or harms.

branches.name: Heterocyclic chemistry
branches.summary: Rings that contain nitrogen, oxygen or sulfur — the skeleton of most drugs.
branches.example: Pyridine, indole and imidazole rings fill medicinal chemistry.

branches.name: Catalysis & organometallics
branches.summary: Metals and small molecules that make bonds form faster, cleaner and more selectively.
branches.example: Palladium cross-coupling joins two carbon fragments in one step.

branches.name: Natural products
branches.summary: Isolating, identifying and making the molecules that plants, fungi and microbes produce.
branches.example: Penicillin and artemisinin both started as natural products.

branches.name: Medicinal chemistry
branches.summary: Designing and optimizing organic molecules into safe, effective drugs.
branches.example: Tuning a lead compound's structure to improve potency and absorption.

branches.name: Polymer chemistry
branches.summary: Linking small organic units into long chains with designed properties.
branches.example: Nylon, PET bottles and biodegradable polylactic acid.

branches.name: Green organic chemistry
branches.summary: Making the same molecules with less waste, safer solvents and less energy.
branches.example: Replacing toxic solvents with water or running reactions solvent-free.

branches.name: Photochemistry
branches.summary: Using light to drive reactions that heat alone cannot.
branches.example: Photoredox catalysis forms bonds at room temperature with visible light.

branches.name: AI & automated synthesis
branches.summary: Machine learning and robots that predict reactions and run experiments.
branches.example: Self-driving labs that choose, run and learn from their own experiments.

timeline.title: The word 'organic' is born
timeline.text: Berzelius names the chemistry of substances from living organisms 'organic'.
timeline.why: The name carried a belief — vitalism — that only life could make these molecules.

timeline.title: Wöhler makes urea
timeline.text: Friedrich Wöhler heats ammonium cyanate, a mineral salt, and gets urea, a molecule from urine.
timeline.why: First crack in vitalism: a 'living' molecule from non-living chemicals.

timeline.title: A failed quinine synthesis gives the first synthetic dye
timeline.text: 18-year-old William Perkin tries to make quinine and gets a purple solid instead: mauveine.
timeline.why: Launched the synthetic dye industry, and with it industrial organic chemistry.

timeline.title: Carbon has four bonds
timeline.text: Kekulé and Couper independently propose that carbon is tetravalent and links to itself in chains.
timeline.why: The birth of structural formulas — the drawings every chemist still uses.

timeline.title: The benzene ring
timeline.text: Kekulé proposes that benzene is a ring of six carbons with alternating bonds.
timeline.why: Opened aromatic chemistry, the basis of dyes, drugs and much of the industry.

timeline.title: Carbon is a tetrahedron
timeline.text: Van 't Hoff and Le Bel independently propose that carbon's four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron.
timeline.why: Explained mirror-image molecules: the start of stereochemistry.

timeline.title: Grignard reagents
timeline.text: Victor Grignard discovers organomagnesium reagents that add carbon to carbonyl groups.
timeline.why: One of the most used C–C bond-forming reactions ever; Nobel Prize in 1912.

timeline.title: The Diels–Alder reaction
timeline.text: Otto Diels and Kurt Alder join a diene and an alkene into a six-membered ring in one step.
timeline.why: Builds rings with full control of 3D shape; Nobel Prize in 1950.

timeline.title: Woodward–Hoffmann rules
timeline.text: Orbital symmetry rules predict which ring-forming reactions are allowed with heat or light.
timeline.why: Turned mysterious 'no-mechanism' reactions into predictable ones.

timeline.title: Retrosynthesis formalized
timeline.text: E. J. Corey formalizes retrosynthetic analysis: plan from the target backwards.
timeline.why: The logic behind modern synthesis planning, now automated by AI; Nobel Prize in 1990.

timeline.title: Olefin metathesis
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Chauvin, Grubbs and Schrock for reactions that swap partners across C=C double bonds.
timeline.why: Cleaner routes to drugs and polymers with less waste.

timeline.title: Palladium cross-coupling
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Heck, Negishi and Suzuki for joining carbon fragments with palladium catalysts.
timeline.why: Now one of the most used bond-forming tools in drug manufacturing.

timeline.title: Asymmetric organocatalysis
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to List and MacMillan for small organic molecules that catalyze one mirror-image form.
timeline.why: Cheaper, greener catalysts without precious metals.

timeline.title: Click chemistry
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Bertozzi, Meldal and Sharpless for fast, reliable snap-together reactions, even inside living cells.
timeline.why: Links molecules like Lego, from drug discovery to labeling cancer cells.

quiz.q: Why can carbon build far more different molecules than any other element?
options: It forms four strong bonds and bonds strongly to itself
It is the most abundant element on Earth
It has the most electrons of the light elements
quiz.explain: Four bonds plus strong C–C bonds let carbon grow chains, rings and branches. Oxygen, not carbon, is the most abundant element in Earth's crust.

quiz.q: In 1828 Wöhler made urea, a 'living' molecule, from which mineral salt?
quiz.explain: Heating ammonium cyanate rearranges it into urea, the same formula, different structure. It undermined the idea that only life can make organic molecules.

quiz.q: An SN2 reaction happens at a stereocenter. What happens to its configuration?
quiz.explain: The nucleophile attacks from the back side, opposite the leaving group, and flips the carbon like an umbrella in the wind (Walden inversion).

quiz.q: An SN1 substitution happens at a stereocenter. What do you mainly get?
quiz.explain: SN1 passes through a flat carbocation that can be attacked from either face, so both configurations form.

quiz.q: Which of these molecules is aromatic?
quiz.explain: Benzene is planar, cyclic, fully conjugated with 6 π electrons (4n+2). Cyclohexane has no π system, cyclooctatetraene folds into a tub, and cyclobutadiene (4 π electrons) is antiaromatic.

quiz.q: Hückel's rule: a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring is aromatic when it holds how many π electrons?
quiz.explain: 2, 6, 10, 14… π electrons fill bonding orbitals completely. 4n rings (4, 8…) are antiaromatic when forced flat.

quiz.q: A Diels–Alder reaction between a diene and a dienophile forms a ring of what size?
quiz.explain: Four carbons from the diene plus two from the dienophile: a cyclohexene ring, formed in one concerted step.

quiz.q: A ketone reacts with a Grignard reagent (RMgBr), then acid workup. The product is…
quiz.explain: The ketone carbon already carries two carbon groups; the Grignard adds a third, and the oxygen becomes OH.

quiz.q: Why must Grignard reagents be kept completely dry?
options: Water protonates the carbon and destroys the reagent
Water makes them explode on contact
Water makes them too reactive to control
quiz.explain: The carbon in R–MgBr behaves like a very strong base. Water simply gives it a proton, turning the reagent into a useless alkane (R–H).

quiz.q: What does 'retrosynthesis' mean?
options: Planning a synthesis backwards from the target to simple starting materials
Running a reaction in reverse in the flask
quiz.explain: You mentally 'disconnect' bonds in the target until you reach purchasable pieces, then run the real reactions forwards.

quiz.q: Two enantiomers (mirror-image molecules) differ in which property?
options: The direction they rotate polarized light
Which atoms are bonded to which
quiz.explain: Enantiomers share every ordinary physical property. They differ only in interactions with other chiral things, like polarized light or enzymes.

quiz.q: Why can two enantiomers of the same drug act differently in the body?
options: Receptors and enzymes are themselves chiral
One of them always decomposes in water
quiz.explain: A chiral receptor fits one mirror image like a right hand fits a right glove; the other enantiomer fits poorly or binds somewhere else.

quiz.q: Which reagent mildly reduces a ketone to a secondary alcohol?
quiz.explain: Sodium borohydride delivers a hydride (H⁻) to the carbonyl carbon. KMnO₄ is an oxidant: it pushes in the opposite direction.

quiz.q: HBr adds to propene. What is the main product?
quiz.explain: H adds to the end carbon so the more stable secondary carbocation forms in the middle; bromide then attacks there (Markovnikov's rule).

quiz.q: The Suzuki coupling joins an organoboron compound and an organic halide with the help of…
quiz.explain: Palladium cycles through oxidative addition, transmetalation and reductive elimination, stitching the two carbons together.

quiz.q: Which group is an ester?
quiz.explain: An ester is a carboxylic acid whose OH is replaced by OR′. R–OH is an alcohol, R–CHO an aldehyde, R–NH₂ an amine.

quiz.q: Which reaction can reach 100% atom economy (every atom ends up in the product)?
options: Substitution that releases a leaving group
quiz.explain: In a Diels–Alder, both reactants combine completely. The Wittig throws away a heavy triphenylphosphine oxide; substitutions lose the leaving group.

quiz.q: A carbon bonded to four different groups is called…
quiz.explain: Four different groups make two non-superimposable mirror arrangements possible: the carbon is a stereocenter.

quiz.q: What is the hybridization of a carbon in a C≡C triple bond?
quiz.explain: Two p orbitals form the two π bonds, leaving one s + one p mixed into two sp orbitals at 180° — alkynes are linear.

quiz.q: Copper-catalyzed click chemistry (CuAAC) joins an azide and an alkyne into…
quiz.explain: The three nitrogens of the azide and two carbons of the alkyne close into a five-membered triazole, fast and almost waste-free.

quiz.q: Which is the most acidic?
quiz.explain: Acetic acid's anion spreads its negative charge over two oxygens (pKa ≈ 4.8). Phenol (≈10) spreads it into a ring less effectively; ethanol (≈16) cannot spread it at all.

quiz.q: In an E2 elimination, the H and the leaving group must usually be…
quiz.explain: Anti-periplanar (180° apart, in one plane) lines up the C–H and C–X orbitals so the new π bond forms smoothly as both groups leave.
